newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Leading candidates take early lead in Bosnia poll.
newsitem.headline: Leading candidates take early lead in Bosnia poll.

text.p: The leading Moslem and Serb candidates for a new collective Bosnian presidency took a substantial early lead over rivals in the country's first post-war elections, organisers said on Monday.

President Alija Izetbegovic was comfortably ahead of former prime minister Haris Silajdzic, his main rival for the Moslem seat in Bosnia's new three-man presidency, by 75 percent to 25 percent, scrutineers said.

International organisers cautioned that the samples counted so far, particularly for the Moslem contest, were too small to indicate reliably whether Izetbegovic would win a big enough majority to ensure he would head the presidency, which will also have Croat and Serb representatives.

In the Bosnian Serb republic, incomplete results from eastern Bosnia showed Momcilo Krajisnik, candidate of the ruling Serb Democratic Party (SDS), had won 83.6 percent of the vote. His nearest rival, Milan Ivanic of the opposition Democratic Patriotic bloc, had 15 percent.
Organisers noted that while east Bosnia is an SDS stronghold, some 70 percent of Bosnian Serbs live in the north.
The first results showed Kresimir Zubak, favoured to win the Bosnian Croat seat, trailing his rival.
Izetbegovic's SDA party feared Silajdzic might take enough votes to let a Bosnian Serb candidate capture the presidency's senior seat.

The results of the contest for the three-man national presidency will not be announced until Tuesday, head of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe's Bosnia mission Robert Frowick told reporters. He said votes were coming in more slowly than expected.
A team of international observers found no major irregularities, its director said in a preliminary report on Monday.

The generally upbeat post-mortem by chief observer Ed van Thijn, Coordinator for International Monitoring, made it likely the OSCE would certify the election outcome despite fraud allegations by parties and voters.

But van Thijn's report was larded with caveats. He said the OSCE should demand the dominant Bosnian Serb separatist party amend its charter to endorse a reunified Bosnia as a condition for validating the elections.

Van Thijn also urged the OSCE not to stage municipal elections later this year as planned unless a problem with rigged voter lists is rectified and freer movement is established across Bosnia's internal ethnic boundaries.
Van Thijn, the Coordinator for International Monitoring in Saturday's elections, said his almost 1,000 observers covered 65 percent of 4,440 polling stations in 87 of 109 districts.
He stressed at a news briefing that his report was preliminary and should be "treated with caution".

"(But), in our opinion, the elections were technically well prepared and carried out successfully under difficult circumstances," he said, alluding to the virulent hostility enduring between Serb, Moslem and Croat communities.

Monitors reported three notable problems with the conduct of the September 14 elections: Names missing or improperly registered at 56 percent of polling stations, polling stations overwhelmed by large crowds of voters and refugees unable to safely reach balloting centres in Serb-controlled areas from which they were evicted in war except along 19 routes guarded by NATO peacekeepers.
Only 14,700 of a possible 150,000 refugees actually crossed communal lines to vote, many for fear of being assaulted. Van Thijn called this figure "very, very disappointing and unacceptable".
